Most conventional licensed seasonal influenza vaccines rely almost exclusively on hemagglutinin, the primary surface glycoprotein of the virus, to induce protective immunity. However, traditional seasonal vaccine formulations often demonstrate suboptimal real-world effectiveness ranging from 20 percent to 60 percent due to ongoing antigenic drift, mismatch between circulating strains and vaccine seed strains, egg-adaptive mutations during manufacturing, and age-associated immune senescence. To overcome these persistent immunologic hurdles, researchers engineered FLUm4HA-4NA, an experimental lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated messenger RNA candidate encoding the full-length hemagglutinin and neuraminidase sequences of four World Health Organization-recommended seasonal influenza lineages, comprising influenza A/H1N1, influenza A/H3N2, influenza B/Victoria, and influenza B/Yamagata. The clinical development program began with a dose-finding phase 1 trial conducted between April 2023 and January 2024 across two clinical sites in Belgium and thirteen sites across the United States. In this first phase, 303 healthy adults aged 18 to 50 years were enrolled, with 293 participants successfully receiving vaccination across thirteen parallel experimental arms. The evaluated formulations encompassed a monovalent construct encoding an A/H1N1 hemagglutinin at an 18-microgram dose, five distinct quadrivalent formulations encoding hemagglutinin alone at varying mRNA concentrations, and six quadrivalent formulations combining both hemagglutinin and neuraminidase mRNAs at different dose ratios, alongside an active comparator cohort receiving the licensed egg-based quadrivalent vaccine Flu Dresden-QIV. Early sentinel cohorts were monitored closely for acute reactogenicity before wider cohort enrollment proceeded, and the initial safety profile revealed no dose-limiting toxicities, deaths, or vaccine-related serious adverse events, confirming that the inclusion of four additional neuraminidase mRNA components did not impair hemagglutinin-specific humoral immunogenicity. Building upon the phase 1 observations, investigators initiated an observer-blind phase 2 trial from October 2023 to July 2024 to evaluate the optimized mRNA candidates across multiple international centers in Belgium, Canada, South Africa, and the United States. The trial stratified participants into two cohorts: younger adults aged 18 to 64 years and older adults aged 65 to 85 years, who typically experience reduced vaccine responsiveness. A total of 480 younger adults and 483 older adults received study injections. Younger adults were randomized to receive one of three FLUm4HA-4NA dose levels containing 3/1 micrograms, 6/2 micrograms, or 9/3 micrograms of hemagglutinin and neuraminidase mRNA per strain, or the standard licensed comparator Flu Dresden-QIV. Older adults received formulations containing 6/2 micrograms, 9/3 micrograms, or 18/6 micrograms per antigen, or the high-dose licensed quadrivalent comparator HD-QIV containing 60 micrograms of hemagglutinin per strain. Discover more Find Vaccines Vaccine vaccines vaccine Get Cold Relief Reactogenicity profiles analyzed across the exposed cohorts showed that solicited local and systemic adverse events occurred more frequently among participants receiving the mRNA formulations than among those receiving licensed egg-derived comparators. In younger adults, solicited adverse events were reported by 84.3 percent to 92.7 percent of mRNA recipients compared with 69.2 percent of licensed comparator recipients, with severe grade 3 symptoms documented in 4.3 percent to 13.9 percent versus 4.2 percent. In older adults, solicited events occurred in 68.9 percent to 72.0 percent of mRNA recipients compared with 53.8 percent of high-dose comparator recipients, with grade 3 symptoms reported in 2.5 percent to 4.1 percent versus 1.7 percent. Injection-site pain was the most common local symptom, while fatigue, headache, and myalgia were the predominant systemic complaints. Symptom severity peaked on day two, and events were transient, with a median duration ranging from one to three days across groups, resolving without lingering clinical sequelae. Systemic safety surveillance over the six-month study period demonstrated an acceptable safety profile across all investigated mRNA dose tiers. Across the phase 2 cohort, unsolicited adverse events occurring within 28 days post-vaccination were reported in 29.6 percent to 43.8 percent of younger adults receiving mRNA formulations compared to 37.5 percent receiving comparator vaccination, while older adult rates ranged from 18.0 percent to 22.4 percent versus 17.1 percent. Unsolicited events deemed related to the study vaccine occurred in 10.4 percent to 21.2 percent of younger adults and 0.8 percent to 10.4 percent of older adults. Over the full 183-day follow-up, serious adverse events were infrequent, and three adverse events of special interest were documented: one case of pericarditis in a younger adult receiving the lowest mRNA dose, one case of hyperthyroidism in a younger comparator recipient, and one case of hyperthyroidism in an older adult receiving the highest mRNA dose. None of these serious events or adverse events of special interest were deemed related to the study vaccination, and no participants withdrew due to adverse events or died. Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology Read Med Journals Assessment of humoral immunity at day 29 revealed distinct antigenic patterns when measuring hemagglutination inhibition antibody titers against homologous seasonal strains. For both influenza A lineages, FLUm4HA-4NA elicited post-vaccination hemagglutination inhibition geometric mean titers and fold-increases that met or exceeded the levels produced by active comparators. In younger adults, adjusted geometric mean titer ratios comparing mRNA groups to the comparator ranged from 1.09 to 1.61 for A/H1N1 and from 1.68 to 2.44 for A/H3N2. In older adults, these ratios ranged from 1.06 to 1.59 for A/H1N1 and from 1.49 to 1.78 for A/H3N2, with titer magnitudes demonstrating a clear dose-dependent increase. Conversely, hemagglutination inhibition responses against the two influenza B strains were lower in the mRNA groups than in the licensed comparator cohorts, yielding adjusted ratios of 0.57 to 0.70 in younger adults and 0.70 to 0.74 in older adults for B/Victoria, and 0.66 to 0.76 in younger adults and 0.69 to 0.84 in older adults for B/Yamagata. In marked contrast to traditional vaccines, which are not standardized or formulated for neuraminidase content, the mRNA candidate induced robust and durable neuraminidase inhibition antibody responses against all four targeted influenza strains. In both younger and older adults, post-vaccination neuraminidase inhibition titers rose sharply following mRNA immunization, whereas responses in the licensed comparator groups were negligible. At day 29, adjusted geometric mean titer ratios comparing FLUm4HA-4NA to comparators ranged from 5.03 to 6.51 in younger adults and 4.29 to 5.96 in older adults for A/H1N1, and from 2.11 to 2.90 in younger adults and 2.20 to 2.69 in older adults for A/H3N2. Elevated ratios were also confirmed for both influenza B strains, ranging from 1.57 to 2.03 in younger adults and 1.49 to 1.95 in older adults for B/Victoria, and from 2.05 to 2.50 in younger adults and 1.70 to 2.12 in older adults for B/Yamagata. Titers remained elevated above baseline through six months post-vaccination across all tested cohorts. Functional antibody evaluations also assessed virus neutralization and cross-reactive humoral breadth against antigenically drifted viral variants circulating around the study period. Microneutralization assays performed on subset cohorts showed that day 29 neutralizing geometric mean titers were comparable or superior to licensed comparators for both influenza A strains and remained above baseline at day 183. When challenged with circulating drifted influenza A strains in hemagglutination and neuraminidase inhibition assays, serum samples from participants vaccinated with FLUm4HA-4NA demonstrated antibody titers that met or exceeded comparator levels. Day 29 neuraminidase inhibition geometric mean titers against drifted A/H1N1 and two drifted A/H3N2 strains significantly surpassed those observed after standard or high-dose comparator vaccination. Tested drifted B/Victoria strains, however, exhibited little to no increase in hemagglutination inhibition titers across either vaccine modality, reflecting the broader challenges of influenza B humoral induction. Cellular immune profiling showed that the mRNA formulations induced coordinated helper and cytotoxic T-cell responses that were largely absent in recipients of licensed split-virion comparator vaccines. Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells collected at day eight demonstrated substantial increases in polypositive CD4+ T cells specific to hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, characterized by the co-expression of at least two activation markers including interferon-gamma, interleukin-2, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. This polypositive response exhibited a pronounced Th1-skewed cytokine polarization, which reflects the classic immune phenotype required for effective viral clearance. Furthermore, vaccination with FLUm4HA-4NA induced hemagglutinin-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell responses in a subset of participants, including older adults across all four strains and younger adults against the influenza B strains, whereas no detectable CD8+ T-cell expansion was elicited by the licensed egg-derived comparators. Memory B-cell analysis corroborated the humoral and T-cell findings, showing an expansion of antigen-specific memory B cells at day eight following mRNA vaccination. Frequencies of memory B cells directed against hemagglutinin from A/H1N1 and A/H3N2 were elevated above comparator levels, while memory B cells directed against B/Victoria were comparable between mRNA and comparator groups. Similarly, neuraminidase-specific memory B cells against A/H3N2 and B/Victoria increased sharply from baseline across the mRNA cohorts and maintained detectable persistence at day 183. These sustained elevations across antibody titers, memory B-cell pools, and antigen-specific T-cell populations indicate that the dual-antigen mRNA platform can establish durable immunologic memory lasting throughout the typical duration of an annual influenza season. The study authors highlighted several structural strengths and methodological limitations inherent in the trial design. Key strengths included the randomized, observer-blind evaluation across multiple geographic regions, the incorporation of age-appropriate licensed active comparators including high-dose quadrivalent vaccine in older adults, and comprehensive profiling spanning humoral, cellular, and cross-reactive endpoints. However, the trial was descriptive without formal hypothesis testing or adjustments for statistical multiplicity, and group sizes in phase 1 were relatively small. Additionally, the study population was predominantly White, which may limit generalizability to other demographic groups, and the trial was designed specifically to measure safety and immunogenicity in medically stable individuals rather than establishing clinical efficacy against laboratory-confirmed influenza illness. Overall, the phase 1/2 trial results confirm that codelivering hemagglutinin and neuraminidase via a sequence-optimized mRNA platform can broaden the antigenic coverage of seasonal influenza vaccines while maintaining an acceptable safety and reactogenicity profile. The ability of FLUm4HA-4NA to stimulate elevated neuraminidase inhibition titers, robust influenza A neutralization, and Th1-biased cellular immunity provides an empirical basis for continued clinical advancement. Future formulation optimization will focus on improving hemagglutination inhibition responses against influenza B lineages and updating antigen selections in accordance with public health guidance, including transitioning to trivalent formulations that omit the extinct B/Yamagata lineage to meet modern global health recommendations. the three-strain trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine (TIV) and the four-strain quadrivalent influenza vaccines (QIVs). TIVs help protect against two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain. QIVs can help protect against four different influenza virus strains, including the two influenza A strains and two influenza B strains. QIVs help reduce the possibility of B strain mismatches, which could result in better protection against the flu, enhanced public confidence and better annual vaccine uptake. Annual immunization is the most effective method of preventing influenza and its complications. The effects of the flu vaccine can wear off, so you need to get a new one every year to stay protected. It’s a simple action that can save lives. Influenza immunization programs focus on three groups of people: those at high risk of influenza-related complications those capable of spreading influenza to individuals at high risk of complications those who provide essential community services With the immunization of nurses, CNA’s position is that they should receive the vaccine each year to protect themselves, their families and those in their care. Read CNA’s Influenza Immunization of Nurses [PDF, 125 KB] position statement for more details. Influenza vaccine 2020-2021 According to the National Advisory Committee on Immunization (NACI), inactivated influenza vaccine and live attenuated influenza vaccine will both be available in Canada for the 2020-2021 influenza season. Also, in anticipation of the circulation of COVID-19 during the fall, NACI has developed guidance on influenza vaccine delivery to help mitigate the risks and provide strategies to address challenges during this influenza season. Canadian immunization guide chapter on influenza and statement on seasonal influenza vaccine for 2020–2021 Guidance on influenza vaccine delivery in the presence of COVID-19 Updated wording for the recommendation on the vaccination of health-care workers NACI has reviewed the wording for the recommendation on the vaccination of health-care workers (HCWs). NACI continues to recommend that HCWs in facilities and community settings should be vaccinated annually against influenza and should remain included in the group who are particularly recommended. Read NACI’s statement for more information. Recommendation on the use of LAIV in HIV-infected individuals NACI has reviewed the evidence and has provided a discretionary recommendation that LAIV may be considered as an option for children 2-17 years of age with stable HIV infection on highly active antiretroviral therapy and with adequate immune function. NACI has concluded that LAIV is immunogenic with this population, and although there is insufficient evidence to detect uncommon or rare adverse events in this context, LAIV appears to have a similar safety profile as inactivated influenza vaccine. Read NACI’s statement for more information. 2020-2021 seasonal influenza campaign The Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) and Immunize Canada provide tools and resources to keep you informed throughout the flu season. The 2026-2027 flu season got off to an early and strong start in the United States, experts say. Influenza activity is still considered low nationally, but cases are rising quickly in many parts of the country, especially in the West. As of Nov. 18, flu infections are growing or likely growing in 34 states, according to the latest estimates from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That’s not unusual, given that flu activity typically ramps up around this time of year. However, this year’s flu season started way ahead of schedule, with infections rising as early as August. “Early-season influenza activity is currently higher than typically observed at this time of year,” the CDC said in its FluView surveillance report for the week ending Oct. 31. So far this season, there have been at least 3,700,000 illnesses, 50,000 hospitalizations and 2,800 deaths from the flu in the U.S., per the CDC. H1N1, a type of influenza A virus, is currently fueling the vast majority of cases. That’s a shift from last winter, when influenza A H3N2 subclade K (aka, the “superflu”) was the dominant strain nationwide. What’s more, it appears that the H1N1 strain circulating in the U.S. has picked up a new mutation which may affect its ability to evade pre-existing immunity, experts say. If H1N1 sounds familiar, that’s because it’s the infamous “swine flu” virus that caused a pandemic in 2009. As the mutated H1N1 strain spreads, doctors are urging people to get the 2026-2027 flu vaccine. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu season and how to protect yourself. Why Is Flu Season Starting So Early? No two flu seasons look the same because the timing and severity can vary from year to year. It’s still too early to tell if this flu season will end up being more severe or what role the mutated H1N1 strain might play, the CDC tells TODAY.com in a statement. However, there are multiple indicators that flu activity is already higher than usual for this time of year. Cases started increasing in late August and early September and have been rising steadily since, per the CDC. The percent of flu tests coming back positive was 11.8% during the week ending Oct. 31. Last year during the same time period, the weekly test positivity rate was about 3%, per the CDC National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System dashboard. Outpatient visits to healthcare providers for flu-like illness hit 3.8% during the week ending Nov. 14, which is higher than the previous two seasons, CDC data show. Hospitalizations and deaths from the flu are also rising. “Cases are still relatively low, so we’re still in the early phases of a flu surge,” Andrew Pekosz, Ph.D., a virologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. As of Nov. 14, 10 states are reporting very high or high levels of flu activity: California, Colorado, Georgia, Louisiana, New Mexico, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington. It’s unclear why exactly cases are rising earlier than normal. One potential reason is that people may have less pre-existing immunity to the H1N1 strain with a new mutation. “Maybe that’s why people are getting sick sooner,” Dr. Bernard Camins, an infectious disease physician and professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, tells TODAY.com. The H1N1 strain spreading is different from the H3N2 strain that dominated last winter. “Even people who got the flu last year are vulnerable,” says Camins. When H1N1 started ramping up in late August, the updated flu shots had just started rolling out. “The pattern we oftentimes see with early season flu is that the first strain that gets here is the one that escapes immunity the most,” Pekosz adds. Does an early flu season mean a more severe flu season? Not necessarily, experts say. “An earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. It’s too early to tell how the 2026-2027 flu season will pan out, or whether it’ll be milder compared to last year’s season. The U.S. saw a harsh flu season last winter fueled by the highly mutated H3N2 subclade K variant, aka the “super flu.” “We still have to see how bad it will be this year, but I think it is just starting earlier,” says Camins. “The only thing predictable about the flu is that it’s unpredictable,” Dr. Natalie Azar, NBC News medical contributor, said on TODAY. What Is the Mutated H1N1 Strain? Influenza viruses mutate constantly, which is why we get an updated flu shot every year. Last summer, flu A H3N2 picked up a host of mutations, which led to the emergence the subclade K variant. H1N1 viruses typically change less often than H3N2 viruses, the CDC says. However, this year, H1N1 (pdm09), subclade D.3.1.1, acquired one new mutation, G155E, says Pekosz. The mutation was first identified in September in Seattle, Washington, according in a preprint paper published to bioRxiv. “It is different from last year’s H1N1 virus, and that mutation position (G155E) we know is important for generating protective antibody responses,” Pekosz explains. This means the latest H1N1 strain may be better able to escape immunity because the antibodies people have from previous infection or vaccination may not recognize it as well. “How that (mutation) is going to affect the disease spread and severity is not clear,” says Pekosz. Even if the H1N1 strain circulating does not match the one included in the 2026-2027 flu vaccines, the shot is still expected to provide protection. “A mismatch is not a black-or-white situation. We may have less immunity, not no immunity,” Pekosz adds. Historically, H1N1 has hit young people particularly hard. The new mutation may make children more susceptible, especially if they haven’t been exposed to H1N1 yet, Azar said. “It is too early to know what viruses may predominate or to say whether there might be implications on flu vaccine effectiveness this season,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. H1N1 Flu Symptoms Influenza often hits suddenly and intensely, says Camins. Common symptoms of the flu include: Fever Chills Fatigue Body aches Runny nose Coughing It can be difficult to distinguish the signs of a flu infection from those caused by COVID-19, which is why testing is important, Camins says. If you test positive for influenza, you can seek treatment with antivirals, which can lessen symptom severity and duration. Antivirals are an especially important tool for high-risk groups, including people over the age of 65, children under the age of 5, and immunocompromised individuals. These medications aren’t available over-the-counter, so you’ll need to see a doctor first. “You have to get that prescription fast ... within the first 48 hours after symptom onset, (or else) they don’t work as well,” says Pekosz. If you experience severe flu symptoms, contact your doctor. When to Get the Flu Shot There’s no reason to panic over the mutated H1N1 strain, the experts emphasize, but it is a good reminder to protect yourself. “View (this) as a a sign to go out and get the flu vaccine,” says Pekosz. Getting a flu shot is the most effective way to prevent against severe illness, complications and death from the flu. The 2026-2027 flu vaccines are available at most pharmacies, doctors’ offices and clinics. The updated shots protect against three viruses: influenza A H1N1 (pdm09), influenza A H3N2 and influenza B. There are multiple options available, including standard flu shots, high-dose shots, a nasal mist and the new mRNA flu vaccine. “Even if there’s a mismatched strain, there’s two other strains that the vaccine will provide better protection against,” says Pekosz. Different flu strains can circulate later in the season, so the shot can protect you throughout the winter and early spring. The flu shot is never 100% effective, Camins adds, and you can still get infected if you’ve been vaccinated — but you won’t get nearly as sick or end up in the hospital. Vaccination is especially important if you’re considered high-risk, but everyone can benefit. The best time to get the flu shot is before the end of October, but the vaccine will still provide protection if you get it later in the season, the experts note. “If you haven’t gotten it yet for whatever reason, now’s the time to get vaccinated because the flu season is starting a little bit sooner and you need at least two weeks for the vaccine immunity to (reach) protective levels,” Pekosz adds. If you aren’t sure which flu vaccine you should get, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, November 24, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Investigational mRNA Flu Vaccine Generates Dual Antigen Immunity in Phase Two Trial by November 19, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Investigational mRNA Flu Vaccine Generates Dual Antigen Immunity in Phase Two Trial Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In a randomized, active-controlled, observer-blind phase 2a clinical study, an investigational mRNA-lipid nanoparticle seasonal influenza vaccine candidate encoding hemagglutinin and neuraminidase antigens elicited robust immune responses against three seasonal influenza strains in younger and older adults. The trial evaluated FLUm3HA-3NA, a trivalent candidate formulated with sequence-optimized messenger RNA encoding hemagglutinin and neuraminidase proteins from influenza A/H1N1, A/H3N2, and B/Victoria strains recommended by the World Health Organization. Primary and secondary endpoint assessments at day 29 demonstrated that all evaluated formulations induced hemagglutination inhibition, neuraminidase inhibition, and virus-neutralizing antibody responses significantly above baseline in both age groups. Across the vaccinated cohorts, the investigational formulations exhibited an acceptable safety profile characterized predominantly by transient, mild-to-moderate reactogenicity, with no vaccine-related serious adverse events or adverse events of special interest identified. These clinical findings demonstrate the feasibility of delivering both major surface viral glycoproteins within a single messenger RNA vaccine platform to broaden seasonal influenza humoral immunity. The development of next-generation influenza vaccines addresses a pressing global public health burden associated with widespread annual morbidity and mortality. Worldwide seasonal influenza epidemics result in an estimated 3.2 million to 9.5 million hospitalizations and between 290,000 and 650,000 respiratory deaths each year. Influenza infection is also linked to acute cardiovascular complications and the exacerbation of underlying chronic pulmonary conditions, amplifying health and economic costs across healthcare systems. While annual vaccination remains the most effective intervention to curb influenza illness, existing licensed seasonal vaccines exhibit suboptimal clinical effectiveness that generally ranges between 20 percent and 60 percent. This substantial variability stems from continuous antigenic drift, mismatches between circulating wild-type strains and selected vaccine strains, and host factors including immunological senescence in older individuals. Furthermore, conventional licensed vaccines produced in embryonated chicken eggs frequently acquire egg-adaptive mutations during manufacturing, compromising structural fidelity with circulating viruses and decreasing real-world protective effectiveness. Messenger RNA vaccine technology provides several distinct structural and manufacturing advantages capable of addressing these traditional vaccine limitations. The mRNA production platform is flexible, scalable, and completely bypasses egg cultivation, thereby eliminating egg-adaptive mutations and reducing strain mismatch risks. Beyond stimulating both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, messenger RNA platforms allow researchers to incorporate multiple distinct antigen-encoding transcripts into a single lipid nanoparticle formulation to broaden protective immunity. Current standard-of-care influenza vaccines target hemagglutinin almost exclusively, leaving neuraminidase unstandardized and often inducing minimal neuraminidase-specific antibody responses. Scientific evidence indicates that antibodies targeting neuraminidase correlate with protection against influenza infection and reduce disease severity independently of hemagglutinin antibodies. Because neuraminidase experiences antigenic drift at a slower rate and independently of hemagglutinin drift, formulating vaccines that encode neuraminidase alongside hemagglutinin represents a promising immunological approach to sustain cross-protection during seasons when hemagglutinin antigens mismatch circulating viral strains. Discover more Find Vaccines Get Cold Relief vaccine vaccines Vaccine The present investigation expanded upon an earlier phase 1/2 clinical study evaluating a quadrivalent candidate, designated FLUm4HA-4NA, which contained mRNA encoding hemagglutinin and neuraminidase for A/H1N1, A/H3N2, B/Victoria, and B/Yamagata strains. That earlier trial demonstrated acceptable safety and immunogenicity, but observed that hemagglutination inhibition responses tended to be higher for influenza A strains and lower for influenza B strains compared with licensed quadrivalent comparators. Because the B/Yamagata lineage has not been detected globally since 2020, the World Health Organization recommended in 2024 that seasonal vaccines exclude the B/Yamagata component. Consequently, the research team designed FLUm3HA-3NA as a trivalent formulation targeting WHO-recommended A/H1N1, A/H3N2, and B/Victoria strains, testing different mRNA dose levels and antigenic ratios to optimize humoral responses across all strains. The randomized, active-controlled, observer-blind phase 2a trial was conducted across 18 clinical centers in the United States under protocol NCT06431607 following ethical approval from the Advarra Institutional Review Board. Conducted under Good Clinical Practice and the Declaration of Helsinki, the trial enrolled medically stable adults with a body mass index between 18 and 35 kg/m2, excluding individuals with confirmed influenza or vaccination within 180 days. Part 1 vaccinated 250 younger adults aged 18 to 64 years and 260 older adults aged 65 to 85 years between May and June 2024 across five cohorts per age group. Younger cohorts received either monovalent FLUmHA containing 24 micrograms of B/Victoria hemagglutinin mRNA, one of three trivalent formulations containing 3 or 6 micrograms of A-strain hemagglutinin mRNA paired with 24 or 48 micrograms of B/Victoria hemagglutinin mRNA and 3 micrograms of each neuraminidase mRNA, or licensed comparator Fluarix Quadrivalent. Older cohorts received one of four trivalent formulations containing 6 or 9 micrograms of A-strain hemagglutinin mRNA, 24 to 72 micrograms of B/Victoria hemagglutinin mRNA, and 3 micrograms of each neuraminidase mRNA, or licensed high-dose comparator Fluzone High-Dose Quadrivalent. Following a protocol amendment, the trial initiated part 2 in November 2024 to evaluate a formulation containing 9 micrograms of A/H1N1 and A/H3N2 hemagglutinin mRNA, 42 micrograms of B/Victoria hemagglutinin mRNA, and 3 micrograms of each neuraminidase mRNA. Part 2 vaccinated 161 younger adults and 162 older adults against licensed trivalent comparators: Fluarix trivalent for younger adults and Fluzone High-Dose trivalent for older adults. Baseline demographic characteristics showed mean ages of 41.9 to 46.3 years for younger adults and 70.3 to 71.6 years for older adults. Female participants accounted for 42.5 to 60.4 percent of younger groups and 56.1 to 66.3 percent of older groups, while White participants comprised 67.9 to 82.0 percent and 79.2 to 95.1 percent, respectively. Prior influenza vaccination within two years was reported by 34.6 to 37.5 percent of younger adults and 70.6 to 73.1 percent of older adults in part 1, compared to 25.9 to 27.5 percent and 41.5 to 42.5 percent in part 2. The primary trial endpoint evaluated day-29 hemagglutination inhibition antibody responses using egg-derived viral strains, with a lower limit of quantification of 10 reciprocal dilutions. In part 1, adjusted geometric mean titers against influenza A strains in FLUm3HA-3NA groups were similar or higher compared with active comparators, yielding adjusted geometric mean titer ratios of 1.10 to 1.66 for A/H1N1 and 1.90 to 2.55 for A/H3N2 in younger adults. In older adults, adjusted ratios reached 1.40 to 1.91 for A/H1N1 and 1.71 to 2.81 for A/H3N2, showing progressive dose responsiveness with higher A-strain mRNA content. For B/Victoria in part 1, adjusted ratios ranged from 0.68 to 1.00 in younger adults and 0.99 to 1.45 in older adults, peaking with highest B/Victoria doses of 48 and 72 micrograms, respectively. In part 2, adjusted ratios for A/H1N1 and A/H3N2 were 1.29 and 1.52 in younger adults and 0.83 and 1.11 in older adults, while B/Victoria ratios were lower at 0.80 and 0.65. In contrast to limited neuraminidase stimulation elicited by licensed egg-based comparators, FLUm3HA-3NA formulations induced robust neuraminidase inhibition responses against all three strains in younger and older adults. Evaluated via enzyme-linked lectin assays in a randomly selected 50 percent subset of participants, day-29 neuraminidase inhibition geometric mean titers and seroconversion rates were markedly higher following mRNA vaccination. Adjusted geometric mean titer ratios between FLUm3HA-3NA and comparator arms across parts 1 and 2 ranged from 8.16 to 11.02 for A/N1, 2.32 to 3.34 for A/N2, and 1.40 to 1.85 for B/Victoria in younger adults. Corresponding ratios in older adults ranged from 5.27 to 8.81 for A/N1, 2.25 to 4.13 for A/N2, and 1.26 to 1.82 for B/Victoria. Conversely, monovalent FLUmHA lacking neuraminidase mRNA yielded ratios below 1.0 against comparators. Additionally, microneutralization assays showed neutralizing titers increased from baseline across all cohorts, with FLUm3HA-3NA producing neutralizing responses similar or higher than comparators for influenza A strains and similar for B/Victoria. Safety analyses in the exposed set showed an acceptable tolerability profile consistent with known mRNA characteristics. Solicited reactogenicity symptoms reported in electronic diaries within 7 days postvaccination occurred more frequently in mRNA cohorts than comparator groups, peaking on day 2 and resolving within 7 days. In part 1, solicited events occurred in 60.0 to 68.0 percent of younger adults and 70.6 to 78.4 percent of older adults receiving mRNA formulations, compared to 54.9 percent and 67.9 percent for comparators, with grade 3 reactions in 0.0 to 7.5 percent. Injection-site pain was the most common local event, while fatigue, myalgia, and headache were the most frequent systemic complaints. Unsolicited adverse events through day 28 were reported at similar rates between groups, with vaccine-related unsolicited events in 0.0 to 6.0 percent of recipients. Serious adverse events reported over 6 months—including Lemierre syndrome, herpes zoster, fractures, and cardiovascular events—were judged unrelated to vaccination, with zero deaths, zero adverse events of special interest, and zero study withdrawals due to adverse events. In discussing the findings, the study authors highlighted that FLUm3HA-3NA demonstrated the biological capacity to induce robust dual-antigen immunity, while acknowledging specific challenges in optimizing influenza B hemagglutinin responses. Lower relative hemagglutination inhibition observed against the B/Victoria strain aligns with findings from multiple mRNA influenza candidates and likely reflects structural issues, such as insufficient prefusion hemagglutinin trimer stability or suboptimal cell-surface expression. Recent investigations demonstrate that targeted antigen redesign can overcome this limitation, confirming that reduced B-strain immunogenicity does not represent an intrinsic defect of mRNA technology. Study authors also noted key study limitations, including its descriptive nature, relatively small cohort sizes, and lack of multiplicity adjustments, which require interpreting conclusions as hypothesis-generating. Furthermore, direct comparisons between part 1 and part 2 remain constrained by differing baseline vaccination histories, distinct comparator vaccines, and updated viral strains. Nonetheless, the substantial induction of neuraminidase inhibition alongside robust influenza A responses supports the ongoing clinical development of multi-antigen mRNA influenza vaccines. These findings, derived from the national framework for influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory infection (SARI), underscore the current epidemiological burden of these pathogens in the region. The study, which utilized RT-PCR testing on respiratory specimens, found an nearly equal distribution between SARI and ILI cases, representing 50.1% and 49.9% of the total cohort, respectively. The majority of individuals seeking care fell within the 16 to 50 age group, accounting for 55.9% of the study population. Through logistic regression analysis, the research team identified age as a significant factor in patient outcomes; specifically, increasing age, alongside pre-existing conditions such as diabetes mellitus, heart disease, chronic respiratory diseases, and chronic hematological diseases, were identified as independent predictors of SARI. Influenza positivity rates showed distinct demographic variations, with the highest prevalence observed among patients aged 6 to 15 years and those with underlying medical comorbidities. While increasing age was independently associated with lower odds of testing positive for influenza, patients suffering from chronic conditions including diabetes, heart disease, respiratory issues, and kidney disease faced significantly higher odds of a positive influenza test. Discover more Get Cold Relief Track Outbreaks Check Symptoms Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Regarding viral circulation, influenza A predominated during the study period, with dominance alternating between the A/H1N1pdm09 and A/H3N2 subtypes. Notably, all identified influenza B cases were classified as belonging to the Victoria lineage, with no evidence found for the circulation of the Yamagata lineage. The recurring winter seasonal pattern for influenza activity emphasizes the critical need for regional health officials to prioritize vaccination campaigns before the peak season begins. The study concludes that enhancing national sentinel surveillance systems and laboratory testing capacity is essential for more accurate detection and ongoing management. By identifying circulating strains and understanding the epidemiological risks posed by specific comorbidities, health authorities can better guide future vaccination strategies and bolster overall public health preparedness against respiratory threats in Iraq. content: China’s flu activity reaches moderate level, with three strains circulating simultaneously: reports Sign in Sign in Subscribe CHINA Politics Society Diplomacy Military Science Odd China Graphic SOURCE GT Voice Insight Economy Comments Company B&R Initiative Biz Graphic OPINION Editorial Observer Asian Review Top Talk Viewpoint Columnists Cartoon HU SAYS IN-DEPTH LIFE Cultural Influencer Attitudes Culture Entertainment Travel WORLD Diplomatic Community SPORT Brasil 247 VIDEO Got-to-watch I-Talk Z-Talk PHOTO Gallery China World Biz Sport INFOGRAPHIC CARTOON CHINA / SOCIETY China’s flu activity reaches moderate level, with three strains circulating simultaneously: reports By GT staff reporters Published: Nov 23, 2026 01:30 PM Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News China's latest influenza surveillance data indicate that flu activity nationwide has reached a moderate level, with three strains circulating at the same time this season, according to media reports. Medical experts said that the flu vaccine offers protection against all three strains, underscoring the importance of boosting vaccination rates and raising public awareness of the vaccine. Northern China has seen a sharp rise in flu positivity rates, while southern regions remain at fluctuating levels of activity, with clustered outbreaks increasing from the previous period, according to data released by the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, CCTV News reported. A notable feature of this year's flu season is the simultaneous circulation of three influenza strains - A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and B(Victoria) - with their respective proportions continuing to shift, the report said. In October, A(H3N2) was overwhelmingly dominant. By November, however, the proportion of A(H1N1) had risen steadily, making it the predominant strain, while A(H3N2) had fallen to below 20 percent. B(Victoria), meanwhile, has maintained a relatively stable share and continued to circulate. The coexistence of multiple influenza strains and the rapid shift in the predominant strain are the most notable features of this year's flu season, posing new challenges for prevention, CCTV said. The risk of being infected by different flu strains in succession has increased, as cross-protection among influenza strains is relatively weak, said Li Tongzeng, a chief physician with the respiratory and infectious diseases department at Beijing You'an Hospital. "For example, contracting influenza A does not rule out a subsequent influenza B infection, while infection with A(H3N2) offers limited protection against A(H1N1), leaving people susceptible to reinfection with a different strain," he added, according to the CCTV report. Li recommended vaccination, noting that the trivalent influenza vaccine offers protection against all three circulating viruses. For the general public, there is little need to focus too much on whether an infection is influenza A or B, as their clinical symptoms are similar, including fever, headache, sore throat, cough, muscle aches and pronounced fatigue, the expert noted. Influenza A and B viruses circulate every year, and existing flu vaccines provide protection against both, President of Shenzhen Third People's Hospital Lu Hongzhou told the Global Times on Monday. The priority in China, therefore, is to increase annual influenza vaccination rates and strengthen public awareness through science-based public health education. Also, existing antiviral medications are effective against both influenza A and B. The key is to obtain an early diagnosis, confirm whether the infection is influenza, and begin treatment promptly, Lu added. content: TOP STORIES HYDERABAD CRIME NATION FACT CHECK Fact Check English Fact Check Telugu Fact Check Tamil Fact Check Kannada Fact Check Malayalam Fact Check Health Now You Know AI/Deepfake What's Next Consumer Voice DATA STORIES SATELLITE JOURNALISM LIFESTYLE HEALTH EDUCATION/JOBS Business / Tech & Startups REGIONAL Andhra Pradesh HYDERABAD SOUTH INDIA TELANGANA Tirupati VISAKHAPATNAM Vijayawada/Amaravati WARANGAL World / NRI News Telugu TOP STORIES FACT CHECK Fact Check English Fact Check Telugu Fact Check Tamil Fact Check Kannada Fact Check Malayalam Fact Check Health Now You Know AI/Deepfake What's Next NATION ENTERTAINMENT LIFESTYLE Go తెలుగు Home REGIONAL HYDERABAD Hyderabad’s viral fever surge: What you need to know about flu and dengue outbreaks Hyderabad’s viral fever surge: What you need to know about flu and dengue outbreaks Atypical symptoms making detection harder By - Kaniza Garari | Published on : 22 Nov 2026 7:39 AM Hyderabad: Hospitals across Hyderabad are reporting a sudden surge in viral fever cases driven by a dual outbreak of seasonal influenza and dengue fever, according to health officials and medical professionals. How did the escalation happen? The co-circulation of Influenza strains A/H3N2 and B alongside dengue has created a challenging clinical situation across outpatient departments. Doctors report that because both illnesses share near-identical symptoms during the initial 48 to 72 hours, many patients are delaying proper medical care, resulting in severe complications by the time they reach emergency rooms. Atypical symptoms making detection harder Dr Srikrishna Raghavendra Boddu, Consultant Physician in General Medicine at Kamineni Hospitals, LB Nagar, warned that dengue is presenting with atypical symptoms this season, making early detection more difficult. Instead of presenting with classic symptoms like sudden high fever and distinct skin rashes, many patients are exhibiting mild fevers accompanied by common flu-like symptoms such as cough, cold, or gastrointestinal discomfort. Also Read - How to use industrial wastewater for urban greenery? HCCB, HMDA show the way According to Dr Boddu, clinicians are observing a rapid drop in blood platelet levels as early as the second or third day of infection, rather than the typical four-to-six-day window seen in classic dengue cases. He emphasised that the critical phase of dengue often occurs after the initial fever subsides, between days three and seven, when the risk of internal fluid leakage and bleeding is highest. At the same time, two distinct influenza strains are spreading rapidly within households. Influenza A (H3N2) is causing sudden high-grade fevers, intense body aches and persistent dry coughs lasting two to three weeks. Meanwhile, Influenza B is leading to fever, muscle pain and prominent gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly among children. Monitoring WBC levels is critical Addressing public concerns over routine blood work, medical experts noted that many patients panic after seeing reduced White Blood Cell (WBC) counts, known as leukopenia, on Complete Blood Count (CBC) reports. Also Read - Illegal human egg donation racket: Telangana HC rejects anticipatory bail pleas of 9 doctors Doctors clarified that a temporary fall in WBC count is a standard reaction to viral infections and does not require antibiotics. However, because falling WBC levels in dengue often precede a drop in platelets, regular blood monitoring remains critical. Symptoms that shouldn’t be ignored Health authorities have identified several key warning signs that require immediate emergency care. For dengue, critical symptoms include: - persistent vomiting - severe abdominal pain - bleeding from the gums or nose - black stools - cold extremities - decreased urine output. For Influenza A, patients should seek immediate help if they experience: - severe breathlessness - chest pain - bluish lips - confusion. For Influenza B in pediatric patients, emergency red flags are: - rapid breathing - refusal to take fluids - seizures - extreme lethargy Medical professionals strongly caution against self-medication and common diagnostic errors that lead to delayed hospital visits. Over-the-counter cold and flu medications can temporarily mask fever spikes while the underlying infection progresses unnoticed. Risk of internal bleeding Furthermore, taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen, diclofenac or aspirin can significantly increase the risk of internal bleeding in dengue patients. Doctors also cautioned against relying on unprescribed antibiotics or substituting clinical monitoring with home remedies such as papaya leaf extract. Early antibody tests, such as dengue IgM tests taken within the first three days, can yield false negatives and provide a false sense of security. Despite the surge in cases, medical experts emphasise that most seasonal viral illnesses resolve smoothly with adequate rest, proper hydration and timely medical guidance. Doctors advise anyone experiencing persistent fever or unusual symptoms to consult a qualified physician promptly rather than self-treating at home. 微信 腾讯QQ QQ空间 中国疾控中心发布的最新监测显示,全国流感活动整体已进入中流行水平,北方流感阳性率上升势头显著,南方维持波动流行状态,聚集性疫情数量较前期有所增加。 今年流感季毒株有何特点?不同人群如何精准防护?孩子得了流感为什么反复高烧?服用抗病毒药物后症状未缓解是怎么回事? 今年流感季 流感毒株有何特点? 今年流感季,流感毒株与往年相比有什么特点?据了解,今年甲型H1N1、甲型H3N2与乙型Victoria系三种毒株同时活跃,且占比持续变动。 今年10月,甲型H3N2毒株流行还占据绝对优势。到了11月,甲型H1N1毒株占比持续走高,成为主流优势毒株,而甲型H3N2毒株已回落到不足两成,乙型Victoria系毒株占比相对稳定,持续流行。 多毒株共存、优势毒株快速切换,是今年流感季最突出的特点,这也给大家防护流感带来了新的挑战,同一流感季先后感染不同毒株的风险加大。 首都医科大学附属北京佑安医院感染综合科主任医师李侗曾介绍,不同流感毒株的交叉保护比较弱,得了甲流之后还有可能再得乙流,得了甲型H3N2之后,对甲型H1N1的保护也比较弱,有可能再得。疫苗是三价疫苗,对三个毒株都有保护作用,可以接种。对普通人群来说,没有必要太介意是甲流还是乙流,临床症状都是相似的,就是发烧、头痛、咽痛、咳嗽、全身肌肉酸痛以及明显乏力。所以大家在预防、判断症状以及治疗上来说,不用太纠结。 儿童和老年人的防护重点 分别是什么? 儿童、老年人是流感的高风险人群,面对今年更复杂的流行态势,他们防护的侧重点分别是什么? 中国疾控中心监测显示,5-14岁的儿童是当前全国流感阳性率最高的年龄组,防护的重点在于“早识别”和“防聚集”。学校与托育机构人员密集,孩子一旦出现发热等症状,不应硬撑上学。班级出现发烧、咳嗽聚集病例时,要及时减少集体活动。 首都医科大学附属北京儿童医院感染内科主任刘钢介绍,当前,儿童任何的呼吸道症状,或原发疾病的加重,或接触流感病例等等,都要考虑到流感的可能性。呼吸道症状可能不是很鲜明,更多的是全身表现,比如肌肉酸痛,或伴有消化道系统的症状。特别要注意1岁以下的小孩,症状更加不特异,可能出现呕吐、腹泻、精神不好等症状。 对于老年人,重点在于“防重症”。65岁以上老年人群大多伴有高血压、糖尿病、慢阻肺等基础疾病,感染流感后极易加重基础病,引发肺炎、心衰等严重并发症。建议符合条件的老年人尽早完成疫苗接种,老人自身如果出现发热,即便症状不重,也建议尽早就诊评估,避免拖延。 李侗曾介绍,比如家里有两个老人,其中一个确诊流感了,另一个老人已经在没有防护的情况下与患者密切接触了,老人本身是重症高风险人群,可以在发生暴露之后,尽快使用奥司他韦进行预防。在预防时,一般一天吃一次,连续用七天就可以。 孩子得了流感为什么反复高烧? 在社交平台上很多家长表示,孩子得了流感反反复复高烧,夜间体温飙升,白天体温稍有回落,持续三四天不见好转,这是什么原因造成的?该如何处理? 专家介绍,和成人不同,儿童流感容易反复高烧,主要原因是儿童的免疫系统尚未发育成熟,病毒入侵后,身体会启动高强度免疫对抗,反应更剧烈,体温波动也比成人更明显。而且流感病毒复制速度快、侵袭性强,会持续刺激身体产生致热物质,导致发热反复。 到了夜间,人体皮质醇分泌减少,免疫力相对下降,病毒活性增强,因此夜间高烧症状会格外突出,尤其儿童体温调节能力弱,相比成人更易出现持续性高热。 北京大学人民医院感染科主治医师王越介绍,从人体发热的机制来讲,还是强调大家应该加强散热。除了在口服退热药物的基础上,会推荐一些物理降温的方法,比如使用一些冰袋,或者用温水擦身子。 专家提醒家长,孩子如果已经安稳入睡且呼吸平稳,不必刻意叫醒喂药,良好睡眠更利于恢复。但如果出现持续嗜睡、呼吸费力、抽搐或退烧后精神依然极差,需立即就医。 服用抗病毒药后症状未缓解 是药物无效吗? 很多患者感染流感后,第一时间服用奥司他韦、玛巴洛沙韦等抗流感病毒药物,但依然持续发烧、咳嗽,是药物无效吗? 首先,抗流感病毒药物的核心作用是抑制病毒复制、缩短病程、降低重症风险,并非即时退烧、立刻止咳的特效药。玛巴洛沙韦在健康儿童中的中位退热时间约为41小时,奥司他韦通常需2-3天才能显现明显改善。在病毒载量被有效压低之前,发热反复是自然病程的一部分。身体已经产生的炎症反应,发烧、咳嗽、乏力等症状会持续一段时间,属于正常恢复过程。 其次,服药时机直接影响恢复效果。流感抗病毒药物最佳服用时间为发病48小时内,越早服用效果越好;如果发病超过两天再服药,病毒已经大量复制,恢复速度会明显变慢,症状缓解自然更迟缓。 王越介绍,有一些病人在临床过程中,可能混合了一些其他情况,比如其他感染。如果混合了其他病原体,就有可能出现症状加重或症状不缓解的情况。针对这种情况,需要重新返回医疗机构,再次完善相应的检查。 关于大家非常关注的流感抗病毒药物耐药问题,中国疾控中心的监测显示,目前国内主流流感毒株,均对奥司他韦、玛巴洛沙韦等一线抗病毒药物高度敏感,大范围耐药情况并未出现。 专家提醒,服用抗病毒药物后无需急于求成,严格遵医嘱、足疗程用药,不擅自停药、换药、加药;规范服药3天至5天后,如果高烧持续不退、咳喘加重,需及时复查,排查是否存在合并感染、并发症等问题,对症调整治疗方案。 流感常合并细菌感染 可自行服用抗生素吗? 很多人刚确诊流感时只是单纯病毒感染,但后期却查出合并细菌感染,比如咳黄痰,甚至出现肺部炎症,这也是流感加重、病程延长的重要诱因。那么,得了流感后,未进行监测可以自行服用抗生素吗? 流感病毒会直接侵袭破坏人体呼吸道黏膜屏障,导致呼吸道黏膜充血、水肿、破损,原本寄居在呼吸道的细菌会大量繁殖。同时,流感感染后,人体免疫力大幅下降,清除病菌的能力减弱,双重作用下,极易诱发细菌性咽炎、扁桃体炎、支气管炎、肺炎等继发感染,老人、儿童、体质虚弱人群风险更高。 王越介绍,如果出现了发热和呼吸道的症状,需要及时到医院进行检测,明确自己到底是不是出现了细菌感染,而不是在家自行口服抗生素。 首先,自行口服抗生素往往没有临床效果,同时还需要承担口服抗菌药物带来的不良反应; 其次,随意口服抗菌药物非常容易出现常见的细菌耐药的情况,对日后出现其他疾病进行诊疗是非常不利的。 认识一下三种毒株 01 甲型H3N2:流感监测中经常出现的名字 H3N2是甲型流感病毒的一个亚型,长期在人群中季节性流行。它的抗原性容易发生变化,既往感染或接种疫苗形成的免疫保护,可能受到影响。因此,去年得过流感,并不意味着今年就可以放心。 既往监测还发现,H3N2占优势的流行季,老年人的流感相关住院和死亡负担往往较重,家中有老年人的家庭尤其要重视防护。 02 甲型H1N1:曾引起大流行,如今也是季节性流感的一员 目前流行的H1N1,也常写作A(H1N1)pdm09。它在2009年引起流感大流行,此后持续在人群中传播,至今已作为季节性流感的一员流行了十余年。H1N1与H3N2虽然都属于甲流,却是不同亚型。得过H3N2,并不能可靠地预防H1N1感染。 03 乙型Victoria系:也是流感,不能因为叫“乙型”就轻视 目前我国流行的乙型流感病毒为Victoria系。“甲型”和“乙型”是病毒分类,并不是病情轻重的排序。乙流同样可以出现高热、头痛、肌肉酸痛和明显乏力,也可能发生肺炎等并发症。 三者引起的症状有很多相似之处,不能仅凭烧得高不高、是否全身酸痛,判断感染了哪一种。 (来源:央视新闻、央视财经) 海量资讯、精准解读,尽在新浪财经APP content_title: Expert: There’s An Unexpected Way the Flu Can Impact Certain People After Recovery
content: For many people, recovering from the flu means waking up without a fever, feeling a little more energetic, and finally getting your appetite back. But for some older adults, shaking the symptoms may be only part of a longer recovery. Health experts say adults 65 and older are at greater risk of serious flu complications, and Samantha Picking, PharmD, senior director of immunizations at Walgreens, says research suggests that a severe case of influenza in older adults can also have lingering effects on strength , mobility, and the ability to carry out everyday activities—especially for those who end up in the hospital. With flu season quickly approaching, we spoke with Dr. Picking to better understand the lesser-known effects of the flu in older adults—and why prevention continues to matter. Why the flu impacts older adults differently Because the immune system can naturally weaken with age, older adults are more susceptible to complications from respiratory illnesses. "The statistics during the 2024 to 2025 season [show that] 71% of seasonal flu-related deaths and 57% of hospitalizations occurred in people 65 years and older," says Dr. Picking. For older adults who are hospitalized with a respiratory illness, the effects can extend beyond the initial infection. In one study of 925 adults 65 and older hospitalized with influenza or another acute respiratory illness, 8.2% experienced persistent moderate functional decline and nearly 10% experienced "catastrophic disability," defined as completely losing independence in at least two basic activities of daily living. "When we look at the research and how this really impacts their lives, it suggests that for some older adults, particularly those who are hospitalized with the flu, recovery can extend beyond those respiratory symptoms," says Dr. Picking. But older adults don't necessarily have to be hospitalized to experience a difficult recovery. Dr. Picking explains that struggling with flu symptoms for seven to 10 days can lead to more time in bed and less eating—which can impact recovery, even after symptoms subside. "Recovery after the flu can then take some time because they may be weaker, they may struggle getting around, and it could take a little bit more time to build that stamina back up," says Dr. Picking. "So it's not always [about] feeling completely better after the flu, but [whether] seniors can get back to their daily lives [as] a really big indicator of how they've recovered." Although the risks increase with age, Dr. Picking emphasizes that older adults should not fear getting the flu. Instead, the research underscores the importance of protecting your health and taking preventative measures —especially since it's impossible to predict how the flu will affect any one person. As Dr. Picking states, "The flu could be mild. The flu could be severe. We just don't know how [it will] impact each of us individually." How everyone can protect their health during flu season Preparing your body for flu season doesn't start in the fall—it's a year-round effort, says Dr. Picking. This means seeing your medical provider regularly, exercising when you can, and maintaining a balanced diet . Sticking with these healthy habits can help support your overall health going into flu season—especially if you have a chronic condition, which can increase the risk of severe flu infections or complications. "[For the] senior population, it's [about] managing your day-to-day to make sure that your body handles something like the flu [being] thrown your way," explains Dr. Picking. Of course, when those flu months do hit, following everyday safety practices can also help, including washing your hands , avoiding close contact with others who are sick, and—most importantly—getting the flu vaccine. "It's [a combination of] factors, but the biggest thing is we have a method to [help] prevent it—and that's the flu vaccine," adds Dr. Picking. She says the best time to get the vaccine is in September or October to help build your immunity through the winter season: "It takes about two weeks to fully build up and develop immunity, so you're getting ahead of the holidays. And if flu starts to peak earlier than expected, you really want to get ahead of that." About the expert Samantha Picking, PharmD , is a licensed pharmacist and the senior director of immunizations at Walgreens. With over a decade of experience, she develops and implements enterprise-wide immunization strategies. content: Skip to content Tuesday, November 24, 2026 Login/Register Home Telangana Hyderabad Andhra Pradesh Real Estate Finance Others Business World Education Top 10 Sports Lifestyle Interviews Gold Rate Today Weather Report Live TV TV 5 Telugu News Live TV9 Telugu News Live V6 News Telugu Live Hyderabad26°C Search Our Menu Home Telangana Hyderabad National Andhra Pradesh Finance Sports Business World Real Estate Education Metro Train Timings Gold & Silver Rate in Hyderabad Hyderabad Weather Today Live TV TV 5 Telugu News Live TV9 Telugu News Live V6 News Telugu Live Hyderabad 26°C Partly Cloudy Login / Register Download Our Apps Download on App Store Get it on Google Play Home > Hyderabad > Hyderabad Hospitals Report Viral Fever Surge As Dengue And Flu Cases Rise Together Hyderabad Hospitals Report Viral Fever Surge As Dengue And Flu Cases Rise Together By Newsdesk Nov 22, 2026, 2:46 PM IST 3 min read Read in English తెలుగు Text size A− 100% A+ Selecteer een taalTelugu Mogelijk gemaakt door Translate Hospitals across Hyderabad are reporting a sudden rise in viral fever cases. Health officials and doctors link the surge to two illnesses spreading together: seasonal influenza and dengue fever. The Influenza A (H3N2) and Influenza B strains are circulating alongside dengue, which has put pressure on outpatient departments. Doctors say both illnesses show near-identical symptoms in the first 48 to 72 hours. As a result, many patients delay proper medical care. By the time they reach emergency rooms, some already have severe complications. Dr Srikrishna Raghavendra Boddu, Consultant Physician in General Medicine at Kamineni Hospitals, LB Nagar, said dengue is showing atypical symptoms this season. Many patients have a mild fever with cough, cold or stomach discomfort, instead of sudden high fever and a distinct skin rash. Doctors are also seeing platelet levels fall as early as the second or third day of infection, rather than the usual four-to-six-day window. He stressed that the critical phase of dengue often begins after the fever subsides, between days three and seven, when the risk of internal fluid leakage and bleeding is highest. Advertisement Discover more Buy Maps News Read Daily News The two flu strains are spreading quickly within households. Influenza A (H3N2) causes sudden high fever, intense body aches and a persistent dry cough that can last two to three weeks. Influenza B brings fever, muscle pain and gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly among children. Doctors also addressed worries over blood reports. A fall in White Blood Cell (WBC) count, called leukopenia, is a standard reaction to viral infections and does not need antibiotics. However, because falling WBC levels in dengue often come before a platelet drop, regular blood monitoring remains important. Health authorities have listed warning signs that need immediate emergency care: Dengue: persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding from the gums or nose, black stools, cold extremities and decreased urine output. Influenza A: severe breathlessness, chest pain, bluish lips and confusion. Influenza B in children: rapid breathing, refusal to take fluids, seizures and extreme lethargy. Medical professionals caution against self-medication. Over-the-counter cold and flu medicines can mask fever spikes while the infection progresses unnoticed. Painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin can raise the risk of internal bleeding in dengue patients. Doctors also advise against unprescribed antibiotics and against replacing clinical monitoring with home remedies such as papaya leaf extract. Dengue IgM antibody tests taken within the first three days can give false negatives. Medical experts say most seasonal viral illnesses resolve with adequate rest, proper hydration and timely medical guidance, and they advise anyone with persistent fever or unusual symptoms to consult a qualified physician promptly. In a... Daily Excelsior 04:02 AM Nov 22, 2026 IST HYDERABAD, Nov 21 : Hospitals in Hyderabad are witnessing a surge in patients with viral fevers, amid the circulation of Influenza A (H3N2), Influenza B and dengue, prompting doctors to advise people against self-medication and delaying medical attention. In a release here on Saturday, Dr Srikrishna Raghavendra Boddu, Consultant Physician, Department of General Medicine, Kamineni Hospitals, LB Nagar, said dengue was presenting with atypical symptoms this season, making early diagnosis and regular monitoring important. Many patients were reporting mild fever, cough, cold and stomach-related problems, mistaking them for ordinary seasonal infections, he said, adding that platelet counts were dropping as early as the second or third day in some dengue cases. He cautioned that the critical phase of dengue could begin after the fever subsided, generally between the third and seventh days, when complications such as fluid leakage and bleeding could occur. He said Influenza A (H3N2) was causing sudden high fever, severe body aches and persistent dry cough, while Influenza B was associated with leg pain, vomiting and loose stools, particularly among children. The infections were also spreading among family members. Dr Boddu said a temporary reduction in white blood cell counts was common in viral infections and did not necessarily warrant antibiotics. However, a declining WBC count in dengue patients could precede a fall in platelet levels, making repeat blood tests and medical supervision essential, he said. Warning against self-medication, he said the use of painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin could increase the risk of bleeding in dengue patients. Unnecessary antibiotics and unsupervised steroid injections could also lead to complications, he also warned.. He advised people not to rely on a single early negative test or discontinue medical follow-up after the fever subsided. Home remedies should not be considered a substitute for medical monitoring, he added. While there was no need for panic as most seasonal infections could be managed with adequate rest, hydration and timely medical care, early consultation and avoidance of self-medication were important to prevent complications, Dr Boddu said. content: 21财经APP 南财号 数字报 越声智投 首页 宏观 公司 金融 证券 全球 观点 汽车 新健康 人文 智库 更多 大湾区 一带一路 文旅 理财 投资通 21视频 直播 品牌活动 首页 医药 正文 流感用药销量翻倍,今冬呼吸道传染病防控有哪些新变化? 2026年11月19日 18:50 21世纪经济报道 21财经APP 闫硕 今冬明春我国呼吸道传染病可能呈现多种病原体交替或叠加流行局面,流感仍是主要呼吸道传染病病原体之一。 21世纪经济报道记者 闫硕 冬春季(一般每年11月至次年3月)是流行性感冒(简称“流感”)等呼吸道传染病的高发季节。中国疾控中心最新通报的监测数据显示,2026年第46周(11月9日—11月15日)南方省份流感病毒检测阳性率略有下降,北方省份流感病毒检测阳性率上升。全国共报告144起流感样病例暴发疫情。 流感相关用药需求同步升温。即时送药平台叮当快药数据显示,甲流、乙流等呼吸道疾病相关用药需求上升。其中北京地区流感药物销量增速更加明显,玛巴洛沙韦近一周(11月9日—11月15日)销量环比增长251%,奥司他韦增长186%。 在中国健康教育中心近日主办的2026冬季流感防控健康科普公益行动启动会上,中国疾病预防控制中心传染病管理处呼吸道传染病预防控制室主任彭质斌表示,当前流感整体在低流行水平波动,但南北方差异较大,今冬明春我国呼吸道传染病可能呈现多种病原体交替或叠加流行局面,流感仍是主要呼吸道传染病病原体之一。 接种流感疫苗是预防流感最有效的手段。相关专家建议所有6月龄及以上且无接种禁忌的人都应接种流感疫苗,医务人员、儿童、老年人、慢性病患者等应优先接种。近期落地的疫苗处方等政策,有望进一步提升接种覆盖率。 2026年第46周流感样病例监测实验室检测结果|来源:中国疾控中心 流感活动呈波动上升趋势 流感是流感病毒引起的急性呼吸道传染病,在我国属于法定丙类传染病。流感病毒可以分为甲(A)、乙(B)、丙(C)、丁(D)四个型别,其中甲型(H1N1亚型和H3N2亚型)和乙型流感病毒会导致每年的季节性流行。 据中国疾控中心监测数据,第45周(11月2日—11月8日)全国哨点医院报告的流感样病例(即发热,腋下体温≥38°C,伴咳嗽或咽痛之一者)占门急诊就诊总数的比例为4.1%。 在流感样病例送检呼吸道样本中,流感病毒阳性率为18.8%,位列第一,较前一周上升3.1个百分点;住院严重急性呼吸道感染病例中,流感病毒阳性率为6.6%,较前一周上升0.6个百分点。流感活动整体呈波动上升趋势。 第46周(11月9日—11月15日)监测数据显示,南方省份哨点医院报告的ILI%(门急诊流感样病例百分比)为4.6%,与前一周水平持平,低于2023年和2025年同期水平(6.4%和6.8%),高于2024年同期水平(3.5%)。 北方省份流感活动有所抬升,哨点医院报告的ILI%为4.5%,高于前一周的3.8%,低于2023年和2025年同期水平(5.9%和7.1%),高于2024年同期水平(3.9%)。 终端用药需求也印证了这一流行趋势。叮当快药数据显示,全国范围内,玛巴洛沙韦近一周(11月9日—11月15日)销量环比增长97%,奥司他韦增长77%,各类退热类产品销量也有一定幅度上涨,例如退热贴销量环比增长28%。同时,平台在北京地区流感药物销量增速更加明显。 值得一提的是,在学校、托幼机构、养老院等人群密集场所,容易出现聚集性疫情。所谓聚集性疫情,即同一地区或单位一周内出现10例及以上流感样病例,经县(区)级疾病预防控制机构核实确认后纳入监测。第46周,全国共报告144起流感样病例暴发疫情,较前一周的125起增长15%。 首都医科大学附属北京儿童医院感染内科主任刘钢指出,儿童是流感的高发群体,也是家庭、校园聚集性疫情的传染源,5岁以下儿童流感发病率高。早产儿、低龄儿及有基础疾病的儿童,是发生肺炎、流感相关脑病等多脏器损伤并发症的高风险人群,需要重点关注。一旦出现流感相关症状,高风险人群要尽早就医,把握48小时治疗窗口,兼顾药物依从性与安全性尽早治疗。符合条件的人群也应积极接种流感疫苗。 把握48小时治疗窗口 流感大多为自限性,少数患者因出现肺炎等并发症或基础疾病加重可发展成重型/危重型病例,可因急性呼吸窘迫综合征、急性坏死性脑病或多器官功能不全等而死亡。 世界卫生组织估计,流感的季节性流行在全球每年可导致300万—500万例重症和29万—65万例呼吸道疾病相关死亡。全球下呼吸道感染疾病负担研究显示,2023年流感导致的下呼吸道感染发病人数位居第二,为2250万例,发病率约为278.8例/10万人次,仅次于肺炎链球菌。 《流行性感冒诊疗方案(2025年版)》明确,有流感重型/危重型高危因素的流感样病例,应尽早进行抗病毒治疗,发病48小时内进行抗病毒治疗获益最大。 目前,我国上市的对流感病毒敏感的药物有神经氨酸酶抑制剂、RNA聚合酶抑制剂和血凝素抑制剂三种。 神经氨酸酶抑制剂以奥司他韦、帕拉米韦、扎那米韦(吸入喷雾剂)等为代表。其中,奥司他韦被市场称为“流感神药”,原研为罗氏的“达菲”,2001年进入国内市场,长期主导国内抗流感药物领域。2016年罗氏相关专利到期后,国内市场格局逐步重构。 摩熵医药数据显示,目前奥司他韦相关产品MAH/生产企业达80家,2025年该品种在医疗机构、实体药店、网上药店的销售额合计超百亿元,达114.48亿元,由东阳光药和罗氏占据主要市场份额。 RNA聚合酶抑制剂以玛巴洛沙韦、法维拉韦等为代表。玛巴洛沙韦也被市场视作新一代抗流感药物,2021年4月在国内获批上市,由罗氏负责商业化,获批8个月后被纳入国家医保药品目录,带动销量快速增长。摩熵医药数据显示,2025年,玛巴洛沙韦片剂和口服液体剂在医疗机构、实体药店、网上药店的销售额合计达19.39亿元。 值得一提的是,2025年以来,国内企业的RNA聚合酶抑制剂相关产品密集获批。科睿药业的玛舒拉沙韦片、众生药业的昂拉地韦片、征祥医药的玛硒洛沙韦片,以及健康元的玛帕西沙韦胶囊陆续获批上市,进一步丰富临床用药选择。 赛道也同步迎来医保政策关键节点,11月14日国家医保局公布新版国家医保目录,玛硒洛沙韦片、玛帕西沙韦胶囊被新增纳入,新版目录将于2027年1月1日正式执行。 血凝素抑制剂代表药物如阿比多尔,国内临床应用相对有限。 相关指南指出,基于多病原流行的现状,在启动抗病毒治疗前,建议及时行病原学检查,以指导治疗。发病时间超过48小时有重型/危重型高危因素的患者和重型/危重型患者,如流感病毒病原学阳性,仍应抗病毒治疗。 在耐药性方面,国家流感中心对2026年3月30日之后送检的部分流感毒株分析发现:全部A(H1N1)pdm09毒株对神经氨酸酶抑制剂敏感;A(H3N2)、B(Victoria)系分别仅有0.2%、0.3%毒株对该类药物敏感性下降,其余毒株均保持敏感;A(H1N1)pdm09、A(H3N2)亚型和B(Victoria)系毒株均对RNA聚合酶抑制剂敏感。 这意味着当前主流抗流感药物对国内流行流感毒株整体仍具备较好的抑制效果,现有抗病毒治疗方案可保持稳定的临床有效性。 接种疫苗为流感防控第一道防线 接种流感疫苗是预防流感最有效的手段,可降低接种者罹患流感和发生严重并发症的风险。 在11月13日国家卫健委召开的新闻发布会上,中国疾病预防控制中心研究员王大燕指出,现在是接种流感疫苗的黄金期,而且越早接种越好。流感疫苗接种后,一般需要2~4周才能产生具有保护水平的抗体,因此最好在当地流感流行季到来前完成接种。但是如果错过了最佳接种时间,也不要担心,整个流感流行季都可以接种。不要认为流感流行季已经开始,接种流感疫苗就没有意义,更不要因此放弃接种。 她同时指出,抗流感病毒药物不能替代流感疫苗,两者的作用方式不同。接种流感疫苗可以刺激人体产生特异性保护抗体,保护作用一般维持6至8个月。而抗流感病毒药物主要通过抑制病毒复制或释放发挥作用,只能提供短期保护,停药后保护作用也会随之消失,不能产生免疫记忆。 世界卫生组织(WHO)及中国国家流感中心公布《推荐2026—2027年北半球流感疫苗组分》,不再纳入B/Yamagata系毒株。因此,本流感季国内不再供应四价流感疫苗,三价流感疫苗成为市场主推产品,其毒株组分包含A(H1N1)pdm09亚型、A(H3N2)亚型和B(Victoria)系。 本年度,我国上市的三价流感疫苗包括三价灭活疫苗(IIV3)和三价减毒活疫苗(LAIV3),其中IIV3有裂解疫苗和亚单位疫苗,可用于6月龄及以上人群;LAIV3适用于3—17岁人群。 中信证券分析近日指出,美国流感疫苗接种水平远高于中国,65岁以上人群接种率近70%,形成较好的群体免疫效果,而国内近年来流感疫苗接种率在3%左右,与美国相比有较大差距,主要系美国疫苗支付体系完善,同时也反映出国内流感疫苗市场潜在成长空间广阔。 多项政策持续推动接种率提升。今年5月,国家医保局和财政部出台有关政策,明确职工医保个人账户可支付定点医疗机构流感疫苗费用;11月,国家疾控局、国家卫生健康委、国家中医药局联合发布《关于全面推行疫苗处方工作的指导意见》,明确了疫苗处方的开具场景、处方主体、服务流程和保障措施,与其他医防融合政策形成组合拳,进一步推动医防融合落地。 中信建投分析指出,近年来浙江、山东、江西等多地疾控、卫健、中医药等部门已开展疫苗处方试点。对浙江疫苗处方项目实施前后社区就诊人群疫苗接种率的研究显示,开具疫苗处方者的流感、肺炎球菌、带状疱疹疫苗接种率分别为79.69%、33.31%、11.13%,均显著高于未开具处方者(58.51%、17.29%、2.96%);多因素分析显示疫苗处方项目干预与三种疫苗接种率均存在正向关联。 <上一篇 rss_summary_html: 【今年流感季优势毒株快速切换】财联社11月22日电，据了解，今年甲型H1N1、甲型H3N2与乙型Victoria系三种毒株同时活跃，且占比持续变动。今年10月，甲型H3N2毒株流行还占据绝对优势。到了11月，甲型H1N1毒株占比持续走高，成为主流优势毒株，而甲型H3N2毒株已回落到不足两成，乙型Victoria系毒株占比相对稳定，持续流行。
